case_study_insert.main_stem: Kestrel Eco-Materials (KEM) is a public limited company in the eco-building-materials sector, employing a workforce of 60 at its recycling plant near Bristol. Founded in 2008 by Priya Kestrel, the business supplies recycled insulation panels to housebuilders and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. KEM plans to invest $780,000 in a low-energy panel-pressing line using recycled glass fibre, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and a $480,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.20 a unit and a selling price of $15.20, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. KEM faces two problems: a defect rate of 4.6% on new panels and rising labour turnover among machine operators.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Report — Q4 2025: The pressing line produced 22,500 insulation panels last quarter with a defect rate of 4.6%, down from 6.1% a year earlier. Customer complaints about panel warping fell from 44 to 19 per month. Average order delivery time is 5.2 days. A survey of 720 housebuilders found that 58% would pay up to $0.60 more for panels made from recycled glass, and 66% require environmental product declarations. Training records show 14 of the 60 operators have not yet had on-the-job training on the new presses; off-the-job certification courses at the technical college cost $1,100 per employee. The operations director is comparing end-of-line quality control inspection with quality assurance based on prevention and team working.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Kestrel Eco-Materials for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Construction Bulletin (February 2026): (1) The central bank has lifted the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, raising debt-service costs on variable-rate borrowing. (2) The national minimum wage will increase by 7.2% from $13.20 to $14.15 per hour from April 2026, pushing up wage bills across the plant. (3) Recycled glass and textile-fibre input prices have risen 11.3% year-on-year, while green-building material inflation is 7.4% and social-housing construction spending has grown 3.8% over the period.

questions.question_text: KEM is funding its $780,000 pressing line partly through a $480,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for KEM of using a share issue instead of the $300,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue brings $480,000 of permanent equity that KEM never has to repay, so the public limited company avoids the interest and capital instalments attached to the $300,000 five-year bank loan. That protects cash flow while the firm carries fixed costs of $270,000 a year and is trying to bring a 4.6% defect rate under control. The money can be tied up in the low-energy panel-pressing line without creating a new monthly commitment that would strain the 90,000-unit operation.

Point 2: Equity also improves the borrowing position for the future: with $480,000 raised from shareholders rather than lenders, KEM has more funds of its own before it approaches a bank, so the balance between borrowed and owned money is less stretched. Priya Kestrel keeps the pressing line in operation even if housebuilders delay orders, because no lender can enforce repayment on the share capital. Although existing shareholders may be diluted, the share issue lets KEM expand into recycled glass fibre panels while the 58% of surveyed housebuilders willing to pay $0.60 more are still being won over.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue over debt identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual analysis of KEM's $480,000 equity, its $300,000 loan and its pressing-line investment.

questions.question_text: KEM is launching recycled insulation panels to housebuilders. Consider advertising in national trade press, sponsoring a green-building conference, or e-mail marketing to existing housebuilder contacts. Which should KEM choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National trade press: Newspapers and trade magazines would give KEM wide visibility among housebuilders and allow technical data on recycled glass fibre panels to be printed in full. This suits a public limited company investing $780,000 in new capacity. However, most readers are outside the Bristol delivery area, response is hard to measure, and the high rates compete with the $270,000 fixed costs and the need to cut a 4.6% defect rate before large orders arrive.

Green-building conference sponsorship: A sponsorship would place KEM beside architects and housebuilders who already care about environmental product declarations, which 66% of the 720 surveyed buyers require. Face-to-face contact builds trust in a new recycled product and can generate specifications. The downside is a large one-off cost, a single event with limited reach, and the risk that competitors at the same conference capture the attention KEM pays for.

E-mail marketing to existing housebuilder contacts: Direct e-mails cost very little, can be targeted at the buyers KEM already supplies, and can carry the 58% survey result about a $0.60 premium and details of the lower defect rate. Delivery is immediate and responses are measurable. Its limits are that it cannot reach new housebuilders, that inboxes are crowded, and that it does little to build the brand needed to fill 90,000 units of output.

Recommendation: KEM should choose e-mail marketing first, with a small conference presence later. E-mail is rejected as the sole long-term answer because it cannot open new accounts, but it wins now because it is cheap, measurable and builds on relationships while the 4.6% defect rate is still being fixed. Trade press is rejected as expensive and unfocused, and full conference sponsorship is rejected as a costly one-off that cannot by itself sustain 90,000 units of sales.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Names the promotional options with limited reference to KEM's product or survey evidence.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of KEM.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in context with a justified recommendation that explains why trade press and sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: KEM's defect rate is 4.6% and labour turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for KEM of using hierarchical leadership with clearly defined quality responsibilities in its pressing plant.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A hierarchical organisational structure gives each press operator a clear place in the chain of command, so responsibility for the 4.6% defect rate can be pinned on a named supervisor rather than shared vaguely. With autocratic leadership, Priya Kestrel can set one standard for panel thickness and enforce it quickly across the 60-operator plant. Fast, unambiguous decisions matter when warping complaints are still 19 a month and the new $780,000 pressing line must be brought up to specification before more housebuilders are supplied.

Point 2: Defined roles and promotion levels give operators a visible career path, which can reduce the rising labour turnover by offering status and higher pay grades within the hierarchy. Keeping experienced staff protects the 22,500 panels made each quarter and avoids the $1,100 per employee cost of off-the-job certification for replacements. Clear responsibilities also make it obvious who must check recycled glass fibre quality, supporting the 66% of surveyed housebuilders who require environmental product declarations and protecting the $480,000 share-issue investment in the new line.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of hierarchical leadership or defined responsibility identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for analysis applied to KEM's defect rate, turnover, training cost and customer requirements.

questions.question_text: KEM must train 14 machine operators on the new pressing line. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job certification at $1,100 per employee. Which should KEM choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at the presses teaches KEM's exact machine settings and quality checks, costs no course fees and allows all 14 operators to keep contributing to the 22,500-panel quarter. Trainers can correct the behaviours behind the 4.6% defect rate the same day, and the method reinforces the team working the operations director is considering. Against that, internal trainers are themselves taken off productive work, bad habits can be passed on, and there is no recognised certificate to show the 66% of housebuilders who want environmental product declarations.

Off-the-job certification: The technical college course at $1,100 per employee costs $15,400 for 14 staff, a small share of the $780,000 investment, and gives an external qualification that strengthens KEM's environmental claims and may help retain staff through a clear progression route. The cost is that 14 of 60 operators are absent from the line during training, which could raise warping complaints beyond 19 a month and worsen the labour-turnover problem if the course feels disconnected from their daily work; the generic content would still need site-specific follow-up.

Decision: KEM should choose on-the-job training as the main method and send a smaller number of senior operators for college certification later. On-the-job training is preferred because it is cheaper, machine-specific and protects output while the defect rate is high; it is not rejected outright, only limited by its lack of formal recognition. Full off-the-job certification for all 14 is rejected now because the $15,400 fee and the loss of 14 of 60 operators would disrupt the pressing line just as KEM tries to stabilise quality and serve the 720 surveyed housebuilders.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with little application to KEM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses advantages and drawbacks of both methods with relevant KEM figures.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Fully evaluates both methods in KEM's context and reaches a justified decision rejecting the alternative.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KEM's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $270,000 ÷ ($15.20 − $9.20) = $270,000 ÷ $6.00 = 45,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 45,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $15.20 − $9.20 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KEM's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 45,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 90,000 units: the margin of safety is 45,000 units, showing how far housebuilder orders could fall before the $780,000 pressing line fails to cover its $270,000 fixed costs.
2. Use the $6.00 contribution per unit to test the survey finding that 58% of housebuilders would pay $0.60 extra: a rise to $15.80 would lift contribution to $6.60, worth 90,000 × $0.60 = $54,000 a year if all panels sold at the higher price.
3. Plan capacity and finance: at 90,000 units total contribution is 90,000 × $6.00 = $540,000, covering fixed costs with $270,000 left for interest on the $300,000 bank loan and for the $480,000 share-issue dividend expectations.
4. Benchmark costs with average total cost of $12.20 ($270,000 ÷ 90,000 + $9.20) and labour productivity of 90,000 ÷ 60 = 1,500 units per worker, so managers can judge whether the 4.6% defect rate or rising labour turnover is pushing unit costs above that level.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 45,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 45,000-unit margin of safety; $0.60 premium modelling worth $54,000; total contribution of $540,000 for finance planning; and unit-cost benchmarking at $12.20 with 1,500 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in each of (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each of four valid applied uses in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KEM's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has KEM's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 14.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 17.5%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $1,250,000 revenue − $750,000 cost of sales = $500,000; 2025 gross profit = $1,500,000 − $825,000 = $675,000. For 2024, $500,000 ÷ $1,250,000 = 0.400; $150,000 operating profit ÷ $1,250,000 = 0.120; $150,000 ÷ $1,000,000 capital employed = 0.150. For 2025, $675,000 ÷ $1,500,000 = 0.450; $210,000 ÷ $1,500,000 = 0.140; $210,000 ÷ $1,200,000 = 0.175.

Evaluation: Revenue rose by 20.0%, from $1,250,000 to $1,500,000, but cost of sales rose by only $75,000, so gross profit jumped from $500,000 to $675,000. This suggests the recycled glass fibre line is winning better prices from housebuilders, consistent with the 58% of surveyed buyers who would pay $0.60 more. Operating profit grew from $150,000 to $210,000, faster than revenue, indicating that the $270,000 fixed costs were absorbed more effectively despite the 4.6% defect rate. ROCE improved from 15.0% to 17.5% even though capital employed increased from $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 for the $780,000 investment, which is a strong signal for shareholders who provided the $480,000 share issue. Interest payable rose from $24,000 to $34,000, so the $300,000 bank loan does absorb some of the gain, but operating profit still comfortably covers it.

Conclusion: KEM's profitability has improved. Every measure moved in the right direction — gross margin 40.0% to 45.0%, operating margin 12.0% to 14.0% and ROCE 15.0% to 17.5% — and the returns rose while the asset base expanded, so the pressing-line investment is adding value rather than merely increasing the scale of the business.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Quotes selected Appendix 2 figures with little accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Calculates the three ratios for both years and describes the trend with some KEM context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for all three ratios in both years plus evaluation of revenue, cost, capital and interest with a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KEM of using recycled glass fibre in its insulation panels.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 720 housebuilders found that 58% would pay up to $0.60 more for panels made from recycled glass and that 66% require environmental product declarations. KEM can therefore support a higher selling price than $15.20 and meet a stated procurement requirement, which helps win specifications from large housebuilders and underpins the $780,000 low-energy pressing line. Higher gross margin also gives more room to absorb the 4.6% defect rate while the new process beds in.

Disadvantage: Recycled glass fibre varies in quality and needs sorting and cleaning, which could push the $9.20 variable cost up and erode the $6.00 contribution per unit if the $0.60 premium is not accepted across all 90,000 units. Inconsistent fibre could also worsen the 4.6% defect rate and the 19 monthly warping complaints, raising waste and threatening the 20% revenue growth recorded in Appendix 2. The 66% of buyers requiring declarations would then have evidence of poor quality rather than environmental benefit.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for development using survey data, price, variable cost, defect rate and investment figures.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 7.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in recycled glass and textile-fibre costs will affect KEM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If the $300,000 five-year bank loan carries a variable rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.0075 × $300,000 = $2,250 a year, a small sum beside $270,000 of fixed costs and $210,000 of operating profit. KEM can also fix the rate or repay part of the loan early using equity from the $480,000 share issue, so this is the least threatening of the three changes even though future borrowing would be dearer.

Minimum wage increase (7.2%, from $13.20 to $14.15 an hour): With a workforce of 60, higher hourly pay raises the plant's wage bill and is unavoidable for eligible staff. The insert supplies no hours worked or individual wage rates, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. The supported comparison is productivity: 90,000 units ÷ 60 workers = 1,500 units per worker. If turnover among machine operators is brought under control and that productivity holds, the cost increase is spread across 1,500 units per worker; if the 4.6% defect rate worsens, unit labour costs rise and the $6.00 contribution is squeezed. The effect is meaningful but can be managed through training and retention.

Input-cost inflation (11.3% on recycled glass and textile fibre): The insert gives $9.20 variable cost per unit but does not decompose it, so an honest upper bound assumes the entire variable cost is exposed: 11.3% × $9.20 = about $1.04 per unit, and on 90,000 units that is roughly $93,600 a year (90,000 × $1.039). Even if only part of the cost is exposed, the impact is large, and it strikes at the same panels whose 45.0% gross margin depends on the $0.60 premium. KEM can pass some of it on to the 58% of buyers willing to pay more, but a 66% requirement for declarations does not guarantee that they will accept a large price rise.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in recycled input costs will have the greatest impact. It touches every panel, can remove around $93,600 of annual contribution on the stated bound and directly threatens the margins that justify the $780,000 investment. The interest rise costs only $2,250 a year and can be fixed; the wage rise can be absorbed through 1,500 units per worker and lower turnover, so neither is as large or as persistent as input-cost inflation.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to KEM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses at least two changes using KEM's figures with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes in context with insert-derived arithmetic and a justified greatest-impact conclusion.
